title: How far should we move the prediction?

beats.say: Start the trace at the job's deadline. We predicted that this large-input job would finish six hours late. The trace keeps going. Twenty hours late. This job has a leaf to itself, so the distance from prediction to finish is its leaf's proposed correction. Fourteen hours.
The learning rate is one quarter. Look at the four equal spaces between the notch and the end of the trace. Where would you put the next prediction?

Nine and a half hours. Move the notch one space. Three and a half hours of the original error are accounted for. Ten and a half remain. The next tree works on the errors left by the trees already fitted. Let's use that idea to flag jobs at risk of missing a deadline.

title: Which jobs can the trees learn from?

beats.say: Start with the jobs from January through March. Their errors tell the trees where to split and how far to move each prediction.
On April jobs, choose how many trees to keep. Then use that model's April scores to choose the alert cutoff.

Freeze those two choices. May shows how the same trees and cutoff handle the next month's jobs. Count the colored squares. May contains fifty-five misses among a hundred and forty jobs. We'll evaluate the frozen pair on those jobs.

title: Make every input and label available in time

beats.say: Boosted trees did well on tables of around ten thousand rows in a twenty twenty-two benchmark. A later Tab P F N study found a competitive neural model on small tables. Our test is about scheduling.
Can the trees catch late jobs more cheaply than a simple alert rule? In these simulated jobs, the large-model flag turns on when input size reaches nine hundred gigabytes.

The heartbeat arrived before the scheduler had to act. The diagnostic arrived afterward, so leave it out. Now look at the training cutoff. A March job still running on April first has no final label yet. It has to wait for a later training run.

Our simulated rows assume those checks have passed. With real logs, join features and outcomes by their arrival times and keep rows from the same incident on one side of the split, or remove the overlap.

What happens if the heartbeat is missing? The classic classifier used here rejects a missing value, or NaN. The scikit-learn histogram gradient boosting classifier learns which way to send missing values.

If the histogram classifier saw no missing values for this feature during training, it uses the child with more training rows. Here there are twelve on the left and five on the right. Which way does the missing heartbeat go?

Left, to the twelve-row child. That tells us where the job goes. Check the scores on jobs with missing telemetry to find out how that population fares. If you impute missing values, fit the imputer on training rows. Test unseen categories separately.

title: A tree fits the remaining error

beats.say: For a transparent first step, predict delay hours for three jobs with a starting value of six. Their actual delays are two, eight, and twenty hours. Subtract the prediction from each outcome to reveal what the current model leaves behind.

The residuals are minus four, plus two, and plus fourteen. Suppose the first two jobs share a leaf and the large-input job has a leaf to itself. The first two errors average to minus one. The other leaf learns plus fourteen. Which way will the prediction for the eight-hour job move?

Down. Move the two markers together. The shared leaf gives both jobs a quarter of minus one hour. Both predictions land at five point seven five. The other leaf adds a quarter of fourteen to six, giving nine and a half. Mean squared error falls from seventy-two to forty-three point one two five hours squared.

Zoom in on the job that took eight hours past its deadline. Its old prediction missed by two hours. Now the gap is two and a quarter. The next tree will see that bigger residual even though the mean squared error fell.

title: Classification trees move a log-odds score

beats.say: The scheduler predicts a label, so the classifier works with a different quantity from delay hours. Its trees add to a raw score called the logit. A sigmoid converts that score to a probability between zero and one. Compute the sigmoid as one divided by the quantity one plus the exponential of the negative logit.

At a logit of zero, the probability is one half. For binary log loss, the derivative with respect to the logit is probability minus the observed label. A missed job pushes the score upward; a job that finishes on time pushes it downward.

To see a fitted update, give the on-time job a leaf and put the two missed jobs together. At even odds the curvature is a quarter per job. Divide the negative sum of gradients by the sum of curvatures in each leaf. The unpenalized moves are minus two and plus two. A half step adds minus one or plus one to the logit. Convert back through the sigmoid. Now the probabilities are about point two seven and point seven three.

title: How much is another leaf worth?

beats.say: For a job that missed, log loss uses the negative log of the probability of a miss. For an on-time job it uses the negative log of the probability of finishing on time. Differentiate with respect to the logit. The first derivative is probability minus label.
For the second, multiply the probability of a miss by the probability of finishing on time. Those are the gradient and the curvature. One half makes the signs easy to see.
The scheduler's fitted classifier actually starts at the training miss rate, a hundred and nineteen out of three hundred and sixty.

Suppose the tree sends several jobs to the same leaf. They all get the same move. Add their gradients to get capital G, and their curvatures to get capital H. The curve shows how X G Boost approximates their change in loss as we vary that move.

Lambda adds a penalty for large weights. At the bottom the slope is zero. Add lambda to H, then divide negative G by that sum to get the weight. That's the best move for these jobs under the quadratic approximation.

Now let one leaf become two. In this example the parent gradients cancel, so its best move saves nothing. Split the jobs. The left gradients sum to minus one and the right gradients sum to plus one. Each side has curvature one.

With lambda one, divide each child's squared gradient by the sum of its curvature and one. Half of that is the saving. Each child saves a quarter. Together they save half a unit. One leaf became two, so charge gamma once.

At a quarter per extra leaf, the net gain is a quarter. A positive gain earns the split in this example. A minimum child size or curvature can still block it, and the learning rate scales the move we actually apply.

Look at the bottom row. The job missed, but the model gave it just a one percent chance. Its gradient is minus point nine nine and its curvature is about one hundredth. Divide by that tiny curvature alone and the proposed weight is a hundred.

Add one to the denominator and the weight falls to about point nine eight. The top row has the same small curvature. Its prediction was nearly right, so its gradient is tiny too. You need both numbers to understand the move. Some configurations also cap the step.

title: Where should this tree split?

beats.say: Here are four training jobs, ordered by one feature and placed in separate bins. The first two missed their deadlines. The others finished on time. In this four-job example the model gave every job a probability of one half. Subtract each label from that probability.

A miss contributes minus one half, an on-time job plus one half. Each contributes a quarter of curvature. In the parent the gradients cancel, and the curvatures add to one. We'll use lambda one and charge nothing for an extra leaf.

Slide the cut just past bin one. That puts a single miss on the left. Its gradient is minus one half and its curvature is a quarter. Subtract that pair from the parent to get the right side. For each side, add one to its curvature.
Divide its squared gradient by that number. Add the two results and halve the sum. The parent term is zero here. The gain is six thirty-fifths, about point one seven one.
The proposed leaf weights are point four on the left and negative two sevenths on the right.

Move one more bin to the left of the cut. Both misses now pull their leaf up. Both on-time jobs pull the other leaf down. Each side has half a unit of curvature, and its gradients add to minus one or plus one.

The middle cut earns two thirds. Its leaf weights are plus and minus two thirds. Try moving the cut after bin three. An on-time job now cancels a miss on the left. The gain falls to six thirty-fifths. Which cut would you keep?
The center cut. Its two leaves separate the misses from the on-time jobs. Multiply their weights by the learning rate before adding them to the logits.

Building a histogram visits the rows for each feature. Once you have totals in the bins, you can scan the boundaries without reading every row again. There's another saving when the tree grows. Keep the parent's histogram and build the left child's. Subtract it bin by bin.

What's left is the right child's gradient and curvature in every bin. With dense data, building costs roughly rows times features. Scanning costs roughly bins times features. Values inside a bin still share one position in the search.

title: A different set of four bins

beats.say: Keep the bins and start again from even odds. This time jobs one and three missed. The labels alternate. Lambda is still one, but now each extra leaf costs a fifth of a unit of gain. The middle cut puts one miss on each side.
The two end cuts each isolate a single job. Does any cut earn enough to pay for that leaf?

Look at the gains before the charge. The middle cut earns zero because the gradients cancel in both children. Each end cut earns six thirty-fifths, just over seventeen hundredths. Subtract a fifth from each candidate. All three lose against the unsplit tree. Keep the parent.
Lower only the leaf charge to one tenth. Now both end cuts clear it by about seven hundredths. Break equal gains in favor of the earliest cut. Split after job one. Follow the right branch.
The third job still has to share its correction with two on-time jobs. The left leaf proposes point four and the right leaf proposes negative two sevenths. Take a quarter step from logit zero.
That gives point one on the left and negative one fourteenth on the right.

Convert those logits back to probabilities. The left branch gets about point five two five. The three jobs on the right get about point four eight two. Put the alert line at point five two. Of the two jobs that actually missed, which one will the operator hear about?

Only job one. Job three is a miss below the line. The split earned a positive gain, but the resulting alerts caught only one of the two misses. We supplied the cutoff for this exercise. For the scheduler, we'll need to choose a policy on later jobs and count what it misses.

title: Change the frontier without changing the loss

beats.say: Separate growth policy from split method. Given one eligible leaf at depth two with gain point four and another at depth three with gain point nine, a closest-to-root depthwise policy expands depth two first. A highest-gain leafwise policy expands depth three first. Depthwise grows level by level.
Leafwise compares gains across all eligible depths, even when you cap the depth. Check the resulting tree on held-out jobs.

X G Boost offers depthwise growth and, with supported approximate or histogram methods, loss-guided growth. Exact splitting scans sorted candidates. Approx uses Hessian-weighted sketches per tree; hist uses a global sketch with supplied sample weights. Feature subsampling has method-dependent support.
Light G B M uses leafwise gain selection; its number of leaves, maximum depth, leaf support and configurable bin count constrain the fitted structure.

CatBoost's symmetric policy applies the same predicate to every node at a given depth. The d predicate outcomes form a binary index into a full table of two to the d leaf values. At depth three, three comparisons identify one of eight leaves.

Read the bits in order. One, zero, one picks leaf five. CatBoost also offers other growth policies. You choose Plain or Ordered boosting separately. Time the full request to see how much this lookup saves on your workload.

title: Sampling rows and encoding categories

beats.say: Gradient-based one-side sampling is an optional Light G B M strategy. Keep the large-gradient group, then sample the small-gradient group with a declared inclusion probability. In a toy with four small-gradient rows sampled independently with probability one half, each retained small row receives inverse-probability weight two.
Individual samples give different totals. Across repeated draws, those weights recover the full sum on average.

Exclusive feature bundling packs sparse columns with little overlap into disjoint bin ranges. If A and B never activate on the same row, zero can represent neither, one can represent A, and two can represent B in a binary toy.
A row with both active breaks that collision-free encoding. When both features can be active, record how the bundle encodes that conflict.

Categorical splits can group categories rather than assume numeric distance between their IDs. Light G B M can order categories by gradient-to-curvature statistics for a partition search; small-cardinality settings may instead use one-versus-rest. CatBoost's ordered target statistic excludes the row's own label.
For three rows sharing one category, with prior one half and smoothing weight one, preceding labels one then zero give the first three rows statistics one half, three quarters, and one half.

In Ordered boosting, look at row three. A model fitted on rows one and two makes its prediction for row three. Suppose it gives the job even odds. Now uncover row three's label. It missed. One minus a half gives a residual of plus one half.

Row three's label first enters the calculation here, after its prediction. Plain boosting can also use the ordered category statistic from the previous example. To see how either model handles future jobs, test it on a later month.

title: Two jobs with the same risk

beats.say: Give both jobs the same chance of missing their deadline. At eight percent risk, we'd expect eight misses for every hundred jobs. The other ninety-two finish on time. An alert costs eight units for each false alarm. Correct decisions cost zero.
Spread those false alarms across all hundred jobs. That averages seven point three six units per job.
What if we stay quiet on a standard job? A missed deadline costs sixty units. Only the eight misses count here. Eight percent of sixty is four point eight. Leave the standard job alone.
Change the tier to priority. A miss now costs a hundred and fifty units. The chance of a miss is still eight percent. Which action costs less for this job?
Eight percent of a hundred and fifty is twelve units for staying quiet. The alert still costs seven point three six. Send the alert.

title: What would an alert cost?

beats.say: What happens if the risk changes? As the true risk rises, follow the yellow line down. A false alarm gets less likely. Staying quiet gets more expensive. The coral line climbs fastest because a missed priority job costs the most.

Where the false-alarm line meets a miss line, the two actions cost the same. Solve for risk by dividing eight by the sum of eight and the miss cost. Alert at a tie. For priority jobs the crossing is just over five percent. For standard jobs it is nearly twelve percent.

Put the risk back at eight percent. An alert costs seven point three six in either tier. Staying quiet costs four point eight for standard and twelve for priority. Those decisions assume a reliable probability and no limit on alert capacity.

On the same hundred and forty April jobs, the heartbeat rule catches forty-eight of fifty-eight misses and raises thirty false alarms. That costs fifteen hundred and sixty units. Try alerting on every job. That catches all the misses. The eighty-two on-time jobs cost eight units each.

That comes to six hundred and fifty-six. Never alerting costs six thousand four hundred and fifty. The booster has to beat the cheaper rule. The heartbeat rule loses to always alerting because priority misses are expensive.

Could a model score go straight onto that risk axis? Take ten jobs that each scored point two. If the score measures risk, we'd expect two misses on average in groups like this. Open the outcomes. Three missed.

Put a dot at point two across and point three up. It sits above the diagonal because the observed share exceeds the forecast. Repeat with other score groups to build a reliability curve. One small group can vary by chance.

The Brier score averages squared probability errors across jobs. Each miss here contributes point six four. Each on-time job contributes point zero four. Average all ten and you get point two two. That measures overall probability error.

If you fit a calibrator, give it rows separate from the ones that fitted the trees, and keep May outside selection. In this scheduler study we use the scores as they are. We'll try one cutoff for both tiers on April and count the actual costs.

title: Validation chooses how many trees to keep

beats.say: A booster can keep adding trees while its training loss improves. The practical question is whether a later month improves too. This seeded fixture trains up to one hundred sixty rounds, then compares each stage on January through March and on April.

Watch the two traces as we read the results from the fitted stages. Both losses fall at first. Put a marker where April's loss is lowest. Will the January through March trace reach its minimum there too?
Training loss continues to fall. April loss turns upward. The lowest April loss is at stage fifty. We paid to train all one hundred sixty stages. We now know how many trees to fit for the candidate.

title: Which model did April select?

beats.say: The search fixes depth two, learning rate point zero five and random seed eleven, then actually trains all one hundred sixty stages. Training loss falls from about point six one six at stage one to point two six eight at stage one hundred sixty.
April loss reaches about point five six four at stage fifty, then worsens to about point five nine two. The selected fifty-stage candidate is refitted on January through March.

Try four stages with validation losses of point six two, point five eight, point five nine and point five eight. Two stages share the minimum. The search keeps the first one. That selects stage two. All four were trained.
The classic classifier's built-in early stopping uses a random stratified slice of the training rows. Scoring each stage on April tests it on a later month.

The threshold must be selected on scores from the resulting candidate. Adding April to the fitting rows changes that candidate and invalidates the old April evidence for its cutoff. A refit needs its own validation rows to choose a cutoff. Here we keep May for the final test of the frozen pair.

title: Find an alert threshold from validation scores

beats.say: A threshold is a gate on a job's score. Take four scores, point two, point six, point six and point nine. Their miss labels are zero, one, zero and one. In this toy, a false alarm costs four and a missed deadline costs ten. Start at point two. Everyone goes through. The two false alarms cost eight. Move the gate to point six. Both tied jobs go through together. We catch both misses and pay for one false alarm, four units. At point nine we miss one deadline and pay ten. Above point nine everyone stays quiet and we pay twenty. The least costly gate passes both tied jobs.

Now use all the scores from the fitted candidate on April. Try every distinct score, along with alerting on everyone and alerting on nobody. At the least costly boundary the gate catches all fifty-eight misses and passes seventy-one on-time jobs. Eight units for each false alarm makes five hundred and sixty-eight.

Open the gate to everyone. We add eleven on-time jobs and catch the same fifty-eight misses. April cost rises to six hundred and fifty-six. April selected both the round count and the cutoff. We'll freeze that pair for May.

title: From the April cutoff to the May queue

beats.say: Each mark is an April job. Start at zero to alert on everyone. Try every distinct score, then the next representable number above one to alert on nobody. Jobs with the same score move together. Choose the lowest total cost, breaking a tie toward the lower cutoff.

Zoom in on the four priority jobs right on the cutoff. Equality sends all four to the operator. Now open their outcomes. Three finished on time, and job ninety-six missed. Each false alarm costs eight. A quiet priority miss costs a hundred and fifty.
The report rounds the cutoff up. Would silencing all four jobs save money?

Keep the stored cutoff first. It catches all fifty-eight April misses. Seventy-one false alarms cost five hundred and sixty-eight units. Eleven on-time jobs stay quiet. Compare the six-decimal number with the stored score. The printed cutoff is slightly higher.

Use the printed cutoff. All four tied jobs go quiet. Three fewer false alarms save twenty-four units, but job ninety-six costs a hundred and fifty as a missed priority deadline. April cost rises to six hundred and ninety-four. That's more than alerting on everyone. Restore the stored cutoff.
The coarse grid started at point one five, where the cost was already thirteen hundred and sixteen.

Carry the exact cutoff and the fifty trees into May. This time there are fifty-five missed deadlines. All fifty-five trigger alerts. The seventy-three false alarms cost five hundred and eighty-four units.

Alerting on every job would cost six hundred and eighty, and the heartbeat rule costs a thousand and forty-four. The candidate saves twelve false alerts, or ninety-six units, while still flagging a hundred and twenty-eight of a hundred and forty jobs.
May's job generator raises each comparable job's risk, but different jobs and random outcomes can still give May fewer misses than April.

title: Why does the quieter rule cost more?

beats.say: Keep the fifty trees and the April cutoff. In May the booster sent a hundred and twenty-eight alerts. The heartbeat rule sent just eighty-one. Which mistakes made the quieter rule more expensive?

Missed deadlines. The heartbeat rule missed three standard jobs and four priority jobs. Those four alone cost six hundred units. That's already more than the booster's entire bill of five hundred and eighty-four. Every unit in the booster's bar comes from a false alarm.

A U C measures how often the model ranks a missed job above an on-time one, giving half credit for ties. At our chosen cutoff we can count the work directly. An operator would have to handle a hundred and twenty-eight alerts.

title: Check support before operating the model

beats.say: An aggregate cost can hide a weak group. On May, the priority slice has thirty-six missed jobs and catches all thirty-six. The large-model slice has thirty-one missed jobs and also catches all thirty-one.

The fixture requires at least ten positive examples in each required slice before its recall check counts. Support gives the recall a useful denominator. A small slice needs more evidence before it can carry a high-stakes decision.

Before operating a booster, bind its feature timing, split, selected rounds, threshold, cost table, slice evidence, and serving schema to one candidate. Then test alert capacity, missing telemetry, rollback, and real request latency. A model is one part of the decision system.

title: Fail a slice on missing support or a policy regression

beats.say: Recall is caught positive jobs divided by all actual positive jobs in the slice. Require ten positives and recall at least point nine for priority, and ten positives and recall at least point eight five for the large-input proxy.

Zero positives gives undefined recall, which fails; nine caught out of nine still fails support. A large priority job counts in both groups. Always alerting would also pass their recall tests. At the priority boundary, nine out of ten passes both inclusive checks.

Keep the trained trees fixed and change only the threshold to point five as a declared stress test. Priority now catches twenty-six of thirty-six positives, about point seven two two. The large-input slice catches twenty of thirty-one, about point six four five. Both fail.
Read the two denominators again. The same thirty-six and thirty-one positive jobs are here. Only the alert cutoff changed. The trained trees and their scores stayed fixed.

Restoring the predeclared frozen threshold reproduces the original evaluation; searching May for a better threshold would consume its final-test role and require fresh evidence. Ten misses let us check recall in this sample. Read that result alongside the cost and the number of alerts the operator would handle.

title: Construct local credit in its stated output units

beats.say: Global gain, split count and impurity decrease summarize different properties and can favor features with many split candidates or redistribute credit among correlated inputs. They do not give the signed contribution to this particular job.
Define a local explanation game with a background population, a missing-feature convention and a chosen model output before computing Shapley credit.

In a separate two-feature game, the empty value is zero, A alone is two, B alone is one, and both give five. In order A then B, the marginal increments are two and three. In order B then A, they are one and four.

Average A's two and four to get three; average B's one and three to get two. Base zero plus those credits reconstructs output five. With more features, Shapley averages across subset orders under the specified game.

Tree S H A P avoids explicit enumeration of all coalitions by propagating path information through each tree. Its path extension and unwinding steps track contributions and coalition-size weights, using branch-cover information for the tree-path-dependent game.

The original bound is order trees times maximum leaves times maximum depth squared. Interventional handling with a background defines a different game; record that choice rather than treating all correlated-feature explanations as identical.

Also record the output units. In a hypothetical raw-logit explanation, base minus one plus point four two and point two six gives minus point three two; sigmoid gives probability about point four two one. The bars add in log odds.
The sigmoid turns their total into a probability. If an escalation flag gets a large share of the credit, check when it was recorded and how fresh it was when the scheduler acted.
To find out whether escalating helps, test its effect on job outcomes in a controlled comparison.

title: Count tree operations and time the complete request

beats.say: Here's April job zero. Its last heartbeat was four hours old. Follow this job through the fifty selected trees. Each leaf changes its running logit. After the last addition its score is about point one zero three.

The search model had a hundred and sixty trees and eleven hundred stored nodes. The selected one has fifty trees and three hundred and fifty nodes. At depth two, that brings the upper bound per job from three hundred and twenty split comparisons to a hundred.
Those counts tell us about tree work. Even a Python interface can run the traversal in compiled code. How much time does scoring take in a whole request?

Trace retrieval, validation and tree scoring under representative load, threads and concurrency. For a separate serial worksheet, eighteen milliseconds of feature work plus two of scoring totals twenty. Suppose a converter cuts scoring to one millisecond. How much of the whole request do we save?

One millisecond out of twenty, or five percent. The request now takes nineteen milliseconds on the worksheet. The eighteen milliseconds of feature work stayed in place. Trace real requests under load to find out which operations overlap and which ones delay the slowest responses.

Treelite exchanges and serializes supported models; its compiler path is T L two c gen. You can also convert a supported estimator to O N N X. Treat conversion, pruning and tree truncation as candidate changes.
Check score and action parity around the full-precision threshold, missing routing and feature order, then recheck quality, slices and actual latency.

Pickle-style Python loading requires trusted sources; inspect supported types with skops and pin the training and loading dependency versions together; loading estimators across different scikit-learn versions is unsupported.

title: Which jobs reach the operator?

beats.say: The scheduler candidate beats both baselines on May and passes its required slice checks. The receipt records how many trees we used, the full cutoff, the cost table, the split and the evaluation. Its checksum starts with F zero zero eight. That identifies this particular JSON record. The release status is still operational checks pending.

Watch one byte of the model change. The receipt stays exactly as it was. To identify what actually served these scores, attach a digest of the fitted model, immutable data and split IDs, the code revision and dependency versions.
Bind the threshold and slice results to those files. Record each feature's meaning, units, arrival time and missing-value rule, plus the names, types, ranges and shapes the server accepts.

Replay two April jobs through the stored rule. Job zero's score is above the cutoff. Job ninety-six's score equals it to the last digit. Both enter the queue. A serving change keeps the cutoff and uses strictly above in place of at or above. Which ticket would disappear?

Job ninety-six. Switch the comparison. Its score stays on the line while its ticket leaves the queue. Job zero still qualifies. The lost ticket belongs to a priority job that missed its deadline. Restore equality. Replay both jobs and both alerts agree. Check feature order, missing-value routing and score parity on representative inputs too.

Before turning on alerts, send the candidate a copy of each request. This shadow run records a score and leaves the job alone. Give it its own resources and access controls. Under realistic load, check the schema, time the full request and practice rollback.
When the deadline passes, pair the score with the outcome. To learn whether acting on an alert helps, test that intervention in a controlled comparison.

Always alerting sent all one hundred and forty May jobs for review. The booster kept twelve on-time jobs out of that queue, leaving a hundred and twenty-eight alerts. Can the operators handle that load? Now try a different decision. Both April tickets qualify and only one review slot is open. Which ticket gets it if higher score goes first?
Job zero. The cutoff put both jobs in the queue. Ranking them by score puts zero ahead of ninety-six.
